readings.title: First reading
readings.text: The word of the Lord was addressed to me as follows: ‘Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel; prophesy and say to them:

exegesis.summary: Through Ezekiel, the Lord indicts the shepherds of Israel who have fed themselves rather than the flock, scattering God's people through neglect and cruelty. The Lord solemnly declares that He Himself will take up the office they abandoned: 'I am going to look after my flock myself.' It is a prophecy of divine intervention that will find its fulfillment in Christ the Good Shepherd.

patristicQuotes.quote: Though the rulers of the Church, those who are her sons and not hirelings, are shepherds, they are all members of that one Shepherd. His office of Shepherd He has permitted His members to bear. But none of us calls himself the door. He could not have added 'good,' if there were not bad shepherds as well.

Our Lord shows here that He did not undergo His passion unwillingly, but for the salvation of the world. He then gives the difference between the shepherd and the hireling: he that is a hireling sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep, and flees.

exegesis.thematicConnection: Ezekiel's promise that God Himself will shepherd His flock is directly answered in Psalm 23 ('The Lord is my shepherd') and consummated in Christ's parable of the vineyard, where the Master personally seeks out laborers and personally pays them, exercising the tender governance the false shepherds refused.

readings.title: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
The Lord is my shepherd: there is nothing I shall want.
The Lord is my shepherd;
there is nothing I shall want.
Fresh and green are the pastures
where he gives me repose.
Near restful waters he leads me,
to revive my drooping spirit.
The Lord is my shepherd: there is nothing I shall want.
He guides me along the right path;
he is true to his name.
If I should walk in the valley of darkness
no evil would I fear.
You are there with your crook and your staff;
with these you give me comfort.
The Lord is my shepherd: there is nothing I shall want.
You have prepared a banquet for me
in the sight of my foes.
My head you have anointed with oil;
my cup is overflowing.
The Lord is my shepherd: there is nothing I shall want.
Surely goodness and kindness shall follow me
all the days of my life.
In the Lord’s own house shall I dwell
for ever and ever.
The Lord is my shepherd: there is nothing I shall want.
readings.refrain: The Lord is my shepherd: there is nothing I shall want.

exegesis.summary: The Church responds to Ezekiel's oracle with the most beloved of pastoral psalms. Where Israel's shepherds failed, the Lord Himself leads to green pastures, walks with the soul through the valley of darkness, and prepares a banquet — a foreshadowing of the Eucharist and the eternal dwelling in the house of the Lord.

patristicQuotes.quote: He that follows Me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life. These words agree with those of the Psalm: 'In Thy light shall we see light, for with Thee is the well of life.' He who shines upon you, that you may see Him, the same flows unto you, that you may drink Him.
Our Lord has acquainted us with two things which were obscure before: first, that He is the Door, and now again, that He is the Shepherd. He enters into the fold by Himself, and we by Him.

exegesis.thematicConnection: The psalm is the flock's grateful answer to Ezekiel's promise: what God pledged through the prophet, the believer now sings as personal experience. Its banquet imagery also anticipates the Gospel, where the Master gives the same wage to all — the fullness of divine generosity, not the scarcity of hirelings.

readings.title: Gospel
readings.text: Jesus said to his disciples: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a landowner going out at daybreak to hire workers for his vineyard. He made an agreement with the workers for one denarius a day, and sent them to his vineyard. Going out at about the third hour he saw others standing idle in the market place and said to them, “You go to my vineyard too and I will give you a fair wage.” So they went. At about the sixth hour and again at about the ninth hour, he went out and did the same. Then at about the eleventh hour he went out and found more men standing round, and he said to them, “Why have you been standing here idle all day?” “Because no one has hired us” they answered. He said to them, “You go into my vineyard too.” In the evening, the owner of the vineyard said to his bailiff, “Call the workers and pay them their wages, starting with the last arrivals and ending with the first.” So those who were hired at about the eleventh hour came forward and received one denarius each. When the first came, they expected to get more, but they too received one denarius each. They took it, but grumbled at the landowner. “The men who came last” they said “have done only one hour, and you have treated them the same as us, though we have done a heavy day’s work in all the heat.” He answered one of them and said, “My friend, I am not being unjust to you; did we not agree on one denarius? Take your earnings and go. I choose to pay the last comer as much as I pay you. Have I no right to do what I like with my own? Why be envious because I am generous?” Thus the last will be first, and the first, last.’

exegesis.summary: Jesus tells of a landowner who hires laborers at every hour and pays each the same denarius, silencing the grumbling of the early workers with a question about His own freedom to be generous. The parable overturns the arithmetic of merit: entrance into the Kingdom is grace, not wages calculated by human reckoning. 'The last will be first, and the first, last.'

patristicQuotes.quote: It is with the first alone that He agrees upon the sum to be given, a denarius; the others are hired on no express stipulation, but 'What is right I will give you.' With the rest He made no contract, seeing He was prepared to give more than the labourers could hope.

The first labourers, having the witness through faith, have not received the promise of God, the Lord of the household providing some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect. And because we have obtained mercy, we hope to receive the reward first.

exegesis.thematicConnection: The landowner in the Gospel is the true Shepherd of Ezekiel and Psalm 23 — the One who personally goes out to seek those 'standing idle' with no one to hire them, just as God went out to seek His scattered sheep. His 'generosity' is the same providential care that prepares a table for us.

synthesis.title: The Shepherd Who Seeks and the Master Who Pays
synthesis.body: Today the Church places before us a single portrait of God drawn in three panels. In Ezekiel, the Lord thunders against shepherds who fattened themselves while the flock scattered, and He announces that He will personally undertake the search: 'I am going to look after my flock myself.' Psalm 23 is the flock's answering song — a soul that has been found, led to green pastures, walked through dark valleys, and seated at a banquet in the house of the Lord forever. Then in the Gospel, we watch that promise put into action. The landowner goes out at daybreak, then at nine, at noon, at three, and even at the eleventh hour, unwilling to leave anyone standing idle in the marketplace. He does not calculate what each has earned; He gives what each one needs to live. As Pseudo-Chrysostom observes, He was 'prepared to give more than the labourers could hope.' This is how the Good Shepherd governs His flock: not as a hireling counting hours, but as a Father whose generosity offends only those who measure grace like wages. The Church invites us today to lay down our envious arithmetic, to receive the denarius of divine life with gratitude, and to trust that the same Shepherd who sought us will seek every soul still standing idle in the world.
